Nepal's flood, start to finish, in the order it happened - and the one claim nearly every headline made that the researchers behind it have since walked back.

On the morning of the disaster, automated software logged the signal as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. It was not an earthquake. The USGS reclassified event us7000tbwb as a landslide, magnitude 5.2 at a depth of zero, and Germany's GFZ Helmholtz Centre independently solved the same instant at 5.2 to 5.7. What came off Langtang Lirung ran roughly 62 miles down the Lhende Khola and the Trishuli, took out dozens of bridges and tens of miles of highway, knocked 431 megawatts of hydropower off Nepal's grid, and buried the Rasuwagadhi crossing into Tibet. More than 700 people are confirmed dead, roughly 2,500 are missing, and the U.S. State Department has at least 90 missing Americans on its list.

Every headline said glacier collapse. The researchers most of those headlines quote have since revised that.

lista.texto: Rajendra Dawadi, principal at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, Nepal got a phone call from a friend who lived in a village miles upriver.  He had narrowly escaped the catastrophe and called his friend, who worked by the river, urging him to evacuate immediately.  Dawadi closed the school for the day and had the teachers escort the students quickly up the nearest hill.  Dawadi was the last one out of the building and barely reached safety when the school and every building nearby were swept away.  That phone call and the quick action of the principal saved over 900 lives in that one town where at least 800 others died.  Sometimes it really does come down to who you know.

I doubt that damming the river played any role. Did the rough math: Initial slope down into the side valley: about 1400 m down, 1580 m distance so roughly 40° on average. The seismic signal happens as the slide hits the valley floor. (Assuming the took the first big spike to timestamp the "earthquake") Side valley to main valley: About 800m down, 5400m distaance, so 6.7° on average. Main valley to border post: about 1200m down, 15500m distance, 3.48° on average. Time to border crossing,  7:40 = 460s, distance 20 900m, so we have a average of 45.43 m/s  There is no way i can see, that the debris flow kind of stopped, made a dam and then had a outburst flood. The gradient in the main valley, shouldn't generate that kind of speed. Neither the one in the side valley. But the water in the river doesn't travel down a 3.48° slope at this speed either. So as the debris flow comes down the valley, it will be like a moving dam showing and absorbing the water of the river. Normally, a debris flow gets pushed by water from behind, it scouring the valley and the front end is like a dam slowing down the movement, while also increasing the height. In this case, because the debris flow traveled so much faster then the water in the river, that water likely lubricated the front end, thereby letting it keep up more momentum.  Can't really find any data..., but basically, up until the moment the debris flow slowed down to roughly the normal flow speed of the river, you have something akin to a reverse outburst flood, where the water gets showed instead of being held back and released.  It's likely the rivers in the main valley got temporary backed up in the aftermath and then released in short order, but that didn't really play a role on the front end of debris flow.
